newsitem.title: GHANA: Ghana gold diggers give mining giants a headache.
newsitem.headline: Ghana gold diggers give mining giants a headache.

text.p: Costly protests by peasant gold diggers ejected from mining land have left Ghana's rapidly growing gold mining sector searching for a solution.

At least five of Ghana's large gold mining firms have reported violent attacks by groups of up to 1,000 armed artisan miners (known locally as "galamsey") in the last 12 months -- and more are expected.
"(Gold mining) is their lifeline so they will never let go," said the manager of a site near Kumasi mined by Bonte Gold Mines, which called out 30 police in February.
"Now we have to keep those 30 policemen on the mine's grounds. That is costing us a fortune," managing director Ben Asare-Quansah told Reuters.
Artisan gold digging was illegal in Ghana until 1989.
Since then, galamsey have taken on global firms licensed to mine open-cast sites over vast tracts of land. They mine where they choose, beyond legal areas, and refuse to move for bigger gold players.
About 30,000 artisan gold diggers accounted for up to 100,000 ounces of Ghana's total output of 1.8 million ounces in 1996, according to World Bank estimates.
Galamsey miners have protested against plans by Bonte Gold Mines' parent company, Akrokeri-Ashanti Gold Mining Inc, to proceed with gold exploration at a nearby site at Jeni.
Police shot two men during a clash at the site.
"There were about 500 men armed with cutlasses and single-barrel shotguns," said Asare-Quansah.

Ashanti Gold Fields Co (AGC) -- West Africa's largest gold miner -- along with Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd, Amansie Resources (Australia), Abosso Goldfields Ltd (Australia) and Bonte have reported attacks over the past year.
Five men were injured and 320 million cedis worth of property destroyed at AGC's Obuasi mine after illegal miners clashed with security forces last March.
About 40 policemen and AGC securitymen tried to drive the illegal miners away from a stockpile of ore at the mine.
In spite of beefed-up security, galamsey miners kept returning, each time to different parts of the vast open-cast mine.
Officials at Ghana's Chamber of Mines, an association of 39 gold producing and exploration companies, believe some galamsey miners receive support from gold dealers.
"The problem is that big gold dealers finance these boys, who have no other option (for work). What we should do is create jobs, like farming and wood processing," said a Chamber spokesman.
Some firms say they have reached compromise solutions with galamsey miners.

In the west Ghanaian town of Damang, Abosso, a subsidiary of Ranger Minerals NL of Australia, is investing $140 million in a carbon-in-leach plant for production by late 1997 of 280,000 ounces of gold per annum.
Police were called to Abosso in October to evict hundreds of illegal galamsey miners from the mine site.
"The police moved in. They (galamsey) became wild. They blocked the road and attacked property and personnel," executive director Mike Ezan told Reuters.

"We realised that we should create harmony in the area. So we appointed a smale-scale mining engineer and registered 740 galamsey who now work in an organised way. They are even policing the area against intrusion by non-registered galamsey," said Ezan.
"They are cooperating very well. This might be the strategy that all mines will have to adopt," he said.
